description: Determine whether target is reachable from start in a directed graph. Nodes have identities 0..nodeCount-1. Each edge row [from,to] permits travel only from from to to; it does not imply a reverse edge.
constraints: 1 <= nodeCount <= 1000. edges has 0..10000 rows of exactly two valid node IDs. Self-loops, duplicate edges, cycles and isolated nodes are allowed. start and target are valid IDs.

A route may have zero edges, so start==target returns true, even for an isolated node. Preserve the edge array, every original row and all values. Graph-node labels/objects are represented by their distinct numeric IDs, not by comparing potentially repeated display labels.
why: Explore only nodes reachable from start. A visited flag set when a node enters the work queue prevents cycles or duplicate edges from causing repeated expansion. If target is encountered it is reachable; exhausting the queue proves no reachable path was omitted.
correctness: Initially start is reachable by the zero-edge path. Every newly queued neighbor extends a known reachable path by one directed edge, so every discovered node is reachable. Conversely, along any path from start, induction on path length shows that expanding the preceding discovered node will discover its next node. Thus every reachable node is eventually discovered. Marking at enqueue time avoids duplicate work without removing any unexplored reachable node. Equality at start handles the explicit zero-edge case; otherwise target is returned true exactly on discovery, and queue exhaustion proves absence.
walkthrough: With edges [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[3,2]], start 0 reaches 1 and then 2, but cannot reach 3 because [3,2] points toward the cycle. Return false for target 3 and true for target 2. With start=target=3 return true without requiring an outgoing edge.
time: O(V+E) time to allocate adjacency/visited storage, read all edges and explore each reachable node/edge at most once.
space: O(V+E) adjacency, visited and queue storage, where V=nodeCount and E=edge count.
edges: An isolated node reaching itself and distinct disconnected nodes.
One-way edges, cycles, repeated edges and self-loops.
A 1000-node chain must not overflow a recursive stack.
related: The author task is directed reachability. Numeric IDs replace wrapper objects, and the zero-edge convention is explicit rather than inheriting the public demonstration's missing start==target check.

description: Return whether the binary subtree rooted at root is height-balanced: at EVERY node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Define empty height as zero and leaf height as one. The empty tree is balanced. This is not a check of root heights alone.
constraints: Displayed tree arguments are {"nodes":[[Data,leftId,rightId],...],"selected":id}. Row indices are distinct node identities; -1 denotes a null link/selection. The table is a valid acyclic binary forest with at most one incoming child link per node. The judge constructs TreeNode objects, connects Left/Right, computes Parent, and passes only the selected TreeNode, not the table. There are 0..1000 rows with signed 32-bit Data, and repeated Data values are allowed unless stated otherwise.

Use the provided TreeNode API (Data,Left,Right,Parent). Preserve every original node object, data value and link, including Parent and unselected nodes. A returned node must be an original object; displayed node results are its row ID, or -1 for null. C++ input nodes are judge-owned and must not be deleted.
Data values do not determine balance; this need not be a search tree. Only the selected root and descendants belong to the checked subtree, even if its Parent is nonnull.
why: A parent needs both child heights, so process nodes in postorder. An explicit enter/exit stack visits children before computing a parent height and avoids recursion-depth failures in a long chain. Store computed heights once and reject any local difference above one.
correctness: When a node exits the stack, both existing children have already exited, so their stored heights are correct by induction; null children have height zero. Taking one plus the larger child height computes the exact node height. If a difference exceeds one, that node witnesses an unbalanced tree. Otherwise each visited node satisfies the defining condition. Every descendant is processed once, so successful exhaustion means every required node is balanced. An initially null root returns true.
walkthrough: A three-node chain with links 0.Left=1 and 1.Left=2 has child heights 1 and 0 at node 1, then 2 and 0 at node 0. The root difference is two, so return false. A deeper violation in either child subtree also causes false even when the root child heights happen to agree.
time: O(n) time for n nodes in the selected subtree: each enters/exits once and has one height computation.
space: O(n) stored node heights plus an O(h) traversal stack for height h; the actual implementation retains completed height entries.
edges: Null root, leaf and two-node tree.
Long skewed chain, equal root heights hiding a deeper violation, repeated Data.
related: The public improved task checks local height differences at every node. The independent implementation uses explicit postorder rather than language recursion.

description: Return whether the selected binary subtree obeys the search-tree rule: every value in a node's left subtree is <= that node's Data, and every value in its right subtree is > it. Duplicates are permitted only on the left side of each relevant ancestor. The empty tree is valid.
constraints: Displayed tree arguments are {"nodes":[[Data,leftId,rightId],...],"selected":id}. Row indices are distinct node identities; -1 denotes a null link/selection. The table is a valid acyclic binary forest with at most one incoming child link per node. There are 0..1000 rows with signed 32-bit Data, and repeated Data values are allowed unless stated otherwise.

Use the provided TreeNode API (Data,Left,Right,Parent). Preserve every original node object, data value and link, including Parent and unselected nodes. A returned node must be an original object; displayed node results are its row ID, or -1 for null. C++ input nodes are judge-owned and must not be deleted.

Check constraints from ALL ancestors, not just immediate children. Parent links outside the selected subtree do not impose additional bounds. Signed endpoints are valid values and must not overflow a bound calculation.
why: Each node inherits a strict lower bound and an inclusive upper bound from its ancestors. Sending the current value as the left upper bound and right lower bound encodes duplicate-left ordering exactly. Widened initial sentinels permit both signed 32-bit endpoints without adding/subtracting one from a node value.
correctness: A stack frame represents all ancestor restrictions as lower<Data<=upper. Root bounds include every signed 32-bit value. A left child inherits the lower bound and upper=parent.Data, enforcing <=; a right child inherits lower=parent.Data and the upper bound, enforcing >. Intersecting inherited bounds carries restrictions through arbitrary depth. Rejecting a bound violation therefore finds a genuine search-tree violation, and if every frame passes then every descendant respects every ancestor restriction, which is precisely the stated BST rule.
walkthrough: For root 5 with a left child 5, the left interval includes its upper bound 5, so equality is valid. A right child 5 fails the strict lower bound. A node 12 inside root 10's left subtree is invalid even if its immediate parent is 5 and 12 is correctly on that parent's right.
time: O(n) time, checking one inherited interval per selected-subtree node.
space: O(h) explicit DFS frames for subtree height h; bounds are signed 64-bit or exact wider host integers.
edges: Equal left versus equal right values, and distant ancestor violations.
Selected internal subtree whose external Parent has unrelated bounds.
related: The author QuestionB explicitly uses lower-exclusive/upper-inclusive bounds; a strict-both-sides or duplicates-anywhere validator would change this exercise.

languageWhy.csharp: C# keeps interval limits as long even though Data is int. The lower sentinel -2147483649 lies outside int range, so int.MinValue remains a legitimate node value without an overflowing Data-1 adjustment.
languageWhy.java: Java record frames store long limits while TreeNode.Data stays int. Comparisons widen Data automatically, preserving the exclusive lower sentinel below Integer.MIN_VALUE and the inclusive Integer.MAX_VALUE upper endpoint.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ frames store long long bounds and compare the signed int Data after safe widening. No unsigned subtraction or Data+1/Data-1 boundary adjustment is used, so both signed endpoints retain their intended ordering.
languageWhy.python: Python exact integers express the lower sentinel below the signed input domain directly. Each immutable frame carries its own inherited limits; a sibling cannot accidentally reuse a bound modified while exploring the other child.
languageWhy.javascript: All Data and bound values, including -2147483649, are exact JavaScript Numbers in this range. The implementation uses ordinary comparisons rather than bitwise coercion, which would wrap that sentinel back into 32 bits.

constraints: Displayed tree arguments are {"nodes":[[Data,leftId,rightId],...],"selected":id}. Row indices are distinct node identities; -1 denotes a null link/selection. The selected node belongs to a valid duplicate-left BST. Its complete component is found through Parent links, rather than treating the selected node as a new root. Return an original TreeNode, not its value, a row index or a newly allocated equal node.
why: If a right subtree exists, inorder next visits its leftmost node. Otherwise the next visit is the first ancestor reached by moving upward from a left child; moving upward from a right child means that ancestor has already been visited. Parent links let this search use constant auxiliary space.
correctness: Inorder visits node's entire right subtree immediately after node, starting at that subtree's leftmost descendant, proving the first case. Without a right subtree, node's own subtree is complete. Every upward right-child edge also completes an ancestor's right subtree, so those ancestors precede node. The first upward left-child edge reaches an ancestor whose left subtree has just completed and whose own visit is next. If no such edge exists, traversal is complete and null is correct. Link comparisons preserve original identity even with equal values.
walkthrough: For rows [[2,1,2],[1,-1,-1],[3,-1,-1]] selecting node 1 (Data=1), it has no right child and is its parent's left child, so return original node 0. Selecting node 0 returns the leftmost node of its right subtree, node 2; selecting node 2 returns null.
time: O(h) link traversals for component height h.
space: O(1) auxiliary pointer storage; no traversal array or cloned node is created.
edges: Null node, root, leftmost/rightmost node and a deep right-subtree left chain.
Equal-valued original nodes and multiple upward right-child edges.

description: Return a build order for projects 0..projectCount-1. A dependency [before,after] requires before to appear earlier than after. Any valid full build order is accepted. Return [] when a dependency cycle makes building every project impossible.
constraints: 0 <= projectCount <= 200. dependencies has 0..10000 rows of two valid project IDs; for zero projects it is empty. Duplicate pairs and self-dependencies are allowed. Preserve the input array, every row and all values.

Every project must occur exactly once in a successful result, including isolated projects. Output order is unrestricted among dependency-respecting full orders. For no projects the valid order is []. Any nonempty cyclic input also returns [], never a partial prefix.
A pair [a,b] means a must be built before b. It does not mean a depends on b. Project numbers represent the original named project identities.
why: A project can be built exactly when all incoming prerequisite edges have been removed. Queue all initially available projects, then emit them and remove their outgoing dependency contributions. A project joins the queue when its last prerequisite contribution is removed, so no repeated scan for available projects is needed.
correctness: Initially each indegree counts all listed prerequisite contributions. Removing a built project decreases exactly its outgoing contributions, so an unbuilt project has indegree zero precisely when all prerequisites have been built. Emitting such a project preserves every dependency. If no candidate exists while projects remain, following remaining prerequisites must revisit a project in the finite graph, proving a cycle; discard the partial prefix and return []. Otherwise every project is emitted exactly once. Every emitted project has no outstanding prerequisite, so their full sequence is a valid build order. Duplicate edges are counted and removed with equal multiplicity.
walkthrough: For four projects with dependencies [[0,2],[1,2],[2,3]], projects 0 and 1 are initially available. The reference queues 0 then 1, making 2 available, then build 3: [0,1,2,3]. Adding [3,1] creates cycle 1->2->3->1, so return [] even though project 0 alone could be built.
time: O(V+E) time: each project enters/exits the queue once, and every listed dependency contribution is read and removed once.
space: O(V+E) adjacency, indegree, emitted flags and output.
edges: No projects, isolated projects and several simultaneously available IDs.
Repeated dependencies, self-dependency, a cycle in only one component and a long chain.
related: The author edge-removal variant establishes prerequisite direction and cycle failure. [] replaces its null failure. The grader accepts every complete dependency-respecting order, including orders different from the reference trace.

description: Return the deepest original node that is an ancestor of both first and second, using provided Parent links. A node is its own ancestor. Return null if either argument is null or if the nodes belong to different trees. No search-tree ordering is assumed.
constraints: Displayed tree arguments are {"nodes":[[Data,leftId,rightId],...],"selected":id}. Row indices are distinct node identities; -1 denotes a null link/selection. The table is a valid acyclic binary forest with at most one incoming child link per node. The judge constructs TreeNode objects, connects Left/Right, computes Parent, and passes only the selected TreeNode, not the table. There are 0..1000 rows with signed 32-bit Data, and repeated Data values are allowed unless stated otherwise.

Use the provided TreeNode API (Data,Left,Right,Parent). Preserve every original node object, data value and link, including Parent and unselected nodes. A returned node must be an original object; displayed node results are its row ID, or -1 for null. C++ input nodes are judge-owned and must not be deleted.

For this shared-identity exercise, the first displayed argument defines the forest and selects first. The second displayed argument is a row ID from that SAME table (or -1), decoded to the original second TreeNode. The callable receives two node objects, not the table or integer IDs.
The forest need not be a BST, and repeated Data values do not identify a node. Use O(1) auxiliary pointer/count storage with the parent-link variant.
why: Count each node's depth and move the deeper node upward until both have equal depth. Then advance both Parent pointers together. Their first meeting is the deepest common ancestor because equal-depth nodes below that meeting are distinct; different tree roots eventually lead both pointers to null.
correctness: Advancing only the deeper pointer cannot skip the common ancestor: every ancestor of the shallower node has depth no greater than that node. After alignment, both pointers are at the same depth. Moving them together preserves this equality and visits ancestors in decreasing depth order. A meeting is therefore common to both original paths, and any deeper common ancestor would have caused an earlier meeting. If their roots differ, they remain distinct until both become null, giving the required absence result. An explicit null-input check prevents treating a nonnull node as an ancestor of null.
walkthrough: In rows [[9,1,2],[9,3,-1],[9,-1,-1],[9,-1,-1]], selecting first node 3 and second node 2 first aligns node 3 upward to node 1. Moving node 1 and node 2 upward together meets at original node 0. All Data values are 9, so value equality cannot solve the identity question.
time: O(h1+h2) Parent traversals for the two component heights.
space: O(1) auxiliary pointers and depth counters.
edges: Either/both null, the same original node and one node already an ancestor.
Different components, equal Data values and very different depths.
related: This is the author's explicit parent-link variant, independently implemented by depth alignment rather than substituting a value-based BST ancestor query.

description: Return whether some node in large roots a subtree identical to small in Data and complete left/right structure. The match includes every descendant and null child position; merely containing the same values or a path is insufficient. The empty small tree is a subtree of every tree, including empty large.
constraints: Displayed tree arguments are {"nodes":[[Data,leftId,rightId],...],"selected":id}. Row indices are distinct node identities; -1 denotes a null link/selection. The table is a valid acyclic binary forest with at most one incoming child link per node. The judge constructs TreeNode objects, connects Left/Right, computes Parent, and passes only the selected TreeNode, not the table. There are 0..1000 rows with signed 32-bit Data, and repeated Data values are allowed unless stated otherwise.

Use the provided TreeNode API (Data,Left,Right,Parent). Preserve every original node object, data value and link, including Parent and unselected nodes. A returned node must be an original object; displayed node results are its row ID, or -1 for null. C++ input nodes are judge-owned and must not be deleted.

Each displayed argument defines its own independent forest and selects its subtree root. Each has at most 1000 rows; repeated values and signed endpoints are allowed. Parent links outside the selected subtree do not participate in matching.
why: Preorder tokens with explicit null markers uniquely describe tree values and shape. Exact token boundaries prevent a value 2 from accidentally matching inside 12. Searching small's complete token sequence inside large's sequence finds a rooted subtree; KMP prefix fallback avoids repeatedly rescanning long repeated-value prefixes.
correctness: A nonnull subtree contributes a contiguous preorder block containing its node token followed by complete left and right blocks; null markers make this encoding uniquely decodable. Thus every actual matching subtree creates a matching token block. Conversely a complete small-tree token match begins at a corresponding node/null token and its null-aware grammar consumes exactly that rooted subtree, so it cannot hide a structural difference or span an incomplete value. KMP preserves the longest pattern prefix matching the consumed suffix and tests every possible start without skipping a token match. Empty small is handled directly as true.
walkthrough: For large rows [[2,1,2],[1,-1,-1],[3,-1,-1]], preorder tokens are [V2,V1,#,#,V3,#,#]. A small leaf 1 has [V1,#,#], which matches. A small root 1 with a left child 3 has different null positions and does not match, even though both values occur in large.
time: O(n+m) token generation and KMP time for n/m selected-subtree nodes. Signed 32-bit value token length is bounded.
space: O(n+m) token strings/prefix table plus explicit traversal stacks; no recursive depth limit is used.
edges: Empty small/large trees, leaf and full-tree equality.
Repeated values, 2 versus 12, mirrored child positions and long chains.
related: The author task requires complete structural matching. The independently authored null-aware token/KMP implementation preserves that task while making numeric and null boundaries explicit.

languageWhy.csharp: C# Stack<TreeNode?> intentionally stores null entries so missing-child positions become tokens. InvariantCulture formats signed values consistently. Keeping node/value tokens in a List<string> prevents matching a digit inside a different integer token.
languageWhy.java: Java uses an ArrayList as a stack because it accepts null children; ArrayDeque would reject them. String.equals compares token contents, and the prefix array follows whole tokens rather than characters in a concatenated number string.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ stores nullable TreeNode pointers in a vector stack and compares complete std::string tokens. A null pointer produces one marker without dereferencing it; decimal conversion stays separate from token boundaries.
languageWhy.python: Python list stacks can retain None child entries, and each produces an explicit marker. KMP compares complete token strings, so value spellings and null positions both participate in structural equality.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript array stacks retain null children. Whole string tokens distinguish numeric values from null markers and from substrings of other values; Number-to-string conversion is exact for the admitted signed integers.

description: Count all nonempty downward paths whose Data values sum to target. A path may start at any selected-subtree node and end at any descendant, following only child links. It need not start at root or end at a leaf, and it cannot go upward or cross between branches.
constraints: Displayed tree arguments are {"nodes":[[Data,leftId,rightId],...],"selected":id}. Row indices are distinct node identities; -1 denotes a null link/selection. The table is a valid acyclic binary forest with at most one incoming child link per node. The judge constructs TreeNode objects, connects Left/Right, computes Parent, and passes only the selected TreeNode, not the table. There are 0..1000 rows with signed 32-bit Data, and repeated Data values are allowed unless stated otherwise.

Use the provided TreeNode API (Data,Left,Right,Parent). Preserve every original node object, data value and link, including Parent and unselected nodes. A returned node must be an original object; displayed node results are its row ID, or -1 for null. C++ input nodes are judge-owned and must not be deleted.

For this exercise every Data is in -1000..1000 and target is in -1000000..1000000. With at most 1000 nodes, all running sums/differences and at most 500500 counted paths fit signed 32-bit integers. Empty root returns zero.

Only the selected root and descendants participate; external Parent links do not extend a path. Count different start/end node occurrences separately, even when their values agree. Empty paths do not count, including for target zero.
why: A downward path ending at the current node has sum target exactly when an earlier prefix sum on the same ancestor path equals runningSum-target. Maintain frequencies of active prefixes, starting with one zero prefix before root. An explicit exit event removes the current prefix before processing a sibling branch, preventing nonexistent cross-branch paths.
correctness: Before entering a node, prefix frequencies count exactly prefixes ending before it on its ancestor chain, including the initial empty prefix. Each occurrence of runningSum-target therefore identifies one and only one nonempty downward path ending here with the desired sum. Counting before inserting the current prefix excludes an empty path. Inserting it makes it available to descendants; its exit event removes exactly that occurrence, restoring the ancestor-only invariant for later siblings. Every path has one endpoint at which it is counted, proving no omission or duplication.
walkthrough: For a three-node chain of zeros and target 0, the successive active zero-prefix counts before insertion are 1,2,3. Those are the numbers of valid paths ending at the three nodes, totaling 6. In a branching tree, removing a finished child's prefix is essential: a path cannot begin in the left branch and end in the right branch.
time: Expected O(n) time with constant-time prefix-frequency dictionary access; hash collisions can worsen the bound.
space: O(h) active prefix frequencies and explicit enter/exit stack for selected-subtree height h; zero-frequency keys are removed on exit.
edges: Null tree, non-root starts, non-leaf ends and negative values.
Zero chains with many overlapping paths and siblings sharing equal prefix sums.
Deep 1000-node paths require explicit stack handling.
related: The author prefix-frequency task permits arbitrary downward start/end nodes. Its recursive entry/exit bookkeeping is independently expressed as explicit events to support deep inputs in every language.
